source.title: Learning a Generative Meta-Model of LLM Activations
source.authors: Grace Luo; Jiahai Feng; T. Darrell; A. Radford; Jacob Steinhardt

page_placements.theme: Selective concept neurons exist and act causally

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies activation modeling and concept probing, but does not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, the prevalence of polysemantic neurons, or whether mixed responses share a feature. Its raw-neuron probe results are related to neuron interpretability but do not test a claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports single-concept probe scores for raw MLP neurons. These measure how well selected neurons predict individual binary concepts, not whether a neuron responds to several unrelated concepts. Recorded those results under versions ["none"]. GLP meta-neuron and dense-probe results were not recorded because they do not measure polysemanticity of individual neurons in the source language models.
record.test_reason: The paper trains a diffusion meta-model of residual-stream activations and evaluates steering and 1-D concept probing. Raw MLP neuron probe AUCs show how well a selected single neuron predicts one binary concept. They do not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, the share of such neurons, its cause, or its dependence on architecture or measurement. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that diffusion meta-models (GLP) of LLM activations scale predictably. As a prior, GLP improves steering fluency. Its meta-neurons isolate concepts better than SAE features or raw neurons on 1-D probes. Raw MLP neurons are the strongest baseline, which the authors read as some native disentanglement. They draw no conclusion about polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a diffusion model of language-model activations and evaluates concept probes; it does not reproduce a polysemanticity measurement or intervention.

fits_no_version.finding: Single raw MLP neurons in Llama1B and Llama8B give 1-D probe AUCs of 0.79 and 0.82 over 113 binary tasks. This beats SAE features and raw layer outputs. The authors call this native disentanglement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some individual LM MLP neurons are well aligned with specific human-labelled binary concepts, more so than SAE latents on single-feature probing.

record.problems: The probe results select the best feature for each task using validation AUC and report aggregate scores over 113 tasks; they do not estimate the proportion of neurons with coherent or mixed functions. The paper does not evaluate polysemanticity directly.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded GLP meta-neuron probe results and dense-probing results: they concern the learned activation model or distributed feature sets, not polysemanticity of individual neurons in the source language models (Tables 4, 10, and 12; Sections 5 and D.2).

untested.parts: No estimate of the share of LM MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no comparison across layers.
No test of superposition as the cause.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
No comparison of polysemanticity across architectures, activation functions or regularization.
Only GLP meta-neuron top-3 examples are inspected; canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
No variation of activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: r3–r6 duplicate r1–r2 numerically (Table 11 vs Table 4). Leaving out GLP meta-neuron results is appropriate: these are the study's own model, not a source LM.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not study image classifiers or mixed responses of vision neurons.
It does not estimate the share of language-model MLP neurons that respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare such a share across layers.
It does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
It does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
It does not compare polysemanticity across architectures, activation functions, or regularization settings.
It examines examples for GLP meta-neurons, not canonical polysemantic neurons in the source language models, and does not test whether mixed responses share a feature.
It does not vary activation range or explanation-scoring methods to assess how polysemanticity measurements depend on those choices.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It reports raw neurons as a baseline and reads their score as 'some native disentanglement'. It neither tests nor uses the claim.

tranche.reason: The paper uses raw MLP neurons only as a 1-D probing baseline for its GLP meta-model. It runs no polysemanticity test: best-neuron AUC does not show whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

source_check.notes: The raw MLP neuron AUCs are mean test AUCs of the best single neuron per task. Neurons come from one middle layer (layer 7 of Llama1B, 8,192 features; layer 15 of Llama8B, 14,336 features), filtered to the top 512 and chosen by val AUC. They say nothing about polysemanticity. Table 11 gives identical values for k=512 and k=all, so r3-r6 duplicate r1/r2. GLP meta-neurons score higher (0.84/0.87).
